extracted.intended_audience: observatory astronomers and meteorologists; scientific instrument operators and readers of the Royal Society (19th-century observational scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for planning, making, reducing, and publishing meteorological and astronomical observations at a scientific observatory (instrumentation, measurement schedules, reductions, and documentation), with emphasis on southern-hemisphere work and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of principal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: THE principal instruments in the Observatory ... are, A 5j-feet transit by Troughton. A 2-feet mural circle by the same. A 16-inch repeating circle by Reichenbach. A 3^-feet telescope with equatorial motion and wire micrometer by Banks. Two instruments for observing the variation and dip of the magnetic needle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the primary instruments used (type, aperture/size, maker) and their intended uses. Explicitly identify makers and dimensions so others can assess instrument capabilities and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan observations with respect to observatory location
rubrics_metrics.description: The observations made with these instruments were planned with particular respect to the place of the Observatory, and confined to what could be done in the southern hemisphere alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the observing programme to exploit the observatory's geographic position (e.g., southern-hemisphere targets) and limit tasks to what can be reliably observed from that site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise measurement types (magnetic first)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first are magnetic observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the prioritisation of observation types (here: magnetic observations given first place) so that essential series are completed and documented in order of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and account for instrument limitations and errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The repeating circle has been in constant use for twenty years, and the nonius of the smaller circle could not be made to close sufficiently to the greater circle. I ascribe it to this cause that the latitudes deduced from some of the observations made with this instrument deviate rather from the truth, the greater part of them having moreover been made without an assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report known defects (e.g., nonius misclosure, flexibility), observing circumstances (e.g., absence of assistant), and how these may bias results. Do not omit problematic observations without consideration; investigate and explain their causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternating direct and reflected observations to check consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The observations made alternately direct and by reflection show on the other hand great consistency; and as the results of these agree with the mean of the observations made with the former instrument on northern and southern stars, there is no doubt of this being the true latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply and report cross-checking observation methods (direct vs reflection) to assess instrument consistency and validate measured quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute latitudes using northern and southern stars and compare
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of latitude in the southern hemisphere could best prove whether the difference usually found between the results derived from stars north of the zenith and those derived from stars south of the zenith, arise from local causes or from imperfections of the instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine latitudes from both north-zenith and south-zenith stars and compare results to diagnose local vs instrumental causes of discrepancies; report reductions and formulas used (e.g., Bohnenberger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate reduction formulae and cite sources
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reductions of these observations, I have partly made use of the formula given by Bohnenberger in his 'Geographische Ortsbestimmung,' § 153.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the mathematical reduction methods and authoritative sources used for processing observations so others can replicate reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain observations that deviate to investigate error sources
rubrics_metrics.description: I might have rejected those observations with the repeating circle that deviated much from the mean; but I was of opinion that the true latitude was not the sole object of importance, but that it was also desirable to investigate the errors arising from flexibility, or causes not sufficiently known, to which repeating instruments are subject ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than discarding outliers automatically, retain and present them when they can reveal instrument behaviours or systematic errors; explain why retained or discarded data were treated as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt reduction methods where usual methods are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The vicinity of the sun to the zenith at the southern solstice rendered the usual methods of reduction insufficient, and a more correct one became necessary, which has already been partly published in the Memoirs of the Astronomical Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When standard reduction techniques fail (e.g., sun near zenith), apply or develop corrected methods and reference prior publications describing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use planetary conjunctions/oppositions and moon culminations for parallax
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of observations of the inferior conjunction of Venus and the opposition of Mars in that part of the world, as well as the culminations of the moon for determining their respective parallaxes, is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan and record observations of specific geometric configurations (Venus inferior conjunction, Mars opposition, moon culminations) to derive parallaxes; document observational circumstances and reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek observations unique to the observatory (comet searches etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was therefore south of the equator that I chiefly searched for comets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect observations of transient or moving objects that are inaccessible to other latitudes to complete global series; document search strategy and time spent, even if unsuccessful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish original observations for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Of these I have given the original observations, in order to enable others to recompute them, to which they are in my opinion well entitled by their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include original/raw observational data (not only reduced results) so others can recompute reductions and verify conclusions; label and format raw data clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose culmination type according to purpose (upper vs lower)
rubrics_metrics.description: The south polar distance of q Argus, β Crucis, and α Eridani, would probably be more correctly deduced from their upper culminations only, with the polar point derived from the other stars, whilst their lower culminations may serve to establish the law of refraction in the southern hemisphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select upper or lower culminations depending on target: use upper culminations for accurate polar distances, and lower culminations to study atmospheric refraction laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local atmospheric effects on refraction
rubrics_metrics.description: It would seem that the effects of the temperature and density of the atmosphere upon the refraction exceed the tabular corrections, which may be owing to a greater elasticity of the air in this warm climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether standard refraction tables are adequate; measure and report temperature/density effects and adjust refraction corrections for local climate when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include derived constants and catalogue entries with aberration and nutation
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion makes a catalogue of the south polar distances of these stars with their constants of aberration and nutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide catalogues of derived positional quantities including associated constants (aberration, nutation) used/applied, so users can understand and reuse the catalogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document instrument heights and installation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Height of the Cistern of the Barometer above a Fixed Mark on Waterloo Bridge. =83 feet 2½ in. ... above the mean level of the Sea (presumed about) . =95 feet. The External Thermometer is 2 feet higher than the Barometer Cistern. Height of the Receiver of the Rain Gauge above the Court of Somerset House. =79 feet 0 in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record precise mounting heights and relative placements (cistern, external thermometer, rain-gauge receiver) and reference fixed marks or mean sea level so that observations can be interpreted and compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: State time standards and observing schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The hours of observation are of Mean Time, the day beginning at Midnight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the time standard used (Mean Time) and the convention for the day (e.g., begins at midnight); specify scheduled observation times (here: 9 A.M. and 3 P.M.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify thermometer and barometer scales and divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thermometers are graduated by Fahrenheit’s Scale. The Barometer is divided into inches and decimals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the temperature and pressure scales and graduations used (Fahrenheit; inches and decimals) so values and conversions are unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record meteorological variables at standard times and with particular columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Meteorological journal columns: 9 o'clock A.M. / 3 o'clock P.M. Barom. Attach. Therm. External Thermometer. Dew Point. Rain, in inches, Read off at 9A.M. Self-registering. Direction of the Wind at 9 A.M. Remarks. Lowest. Highest. Mean and sum values presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a consistent tabular format recording barometer and thermometer readings at standard times (9AM and 3PM), dew point, rain (in inches, read at 9AM), wind direction, lowest/highest readings and include remarks; use self-registering instruments where appropriate and provide monthly means and sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct barometer readings for capillarity and standard temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Monthly Mean of the Barometer, corrected for Capillarity and reduced to 32° Fahr.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply corrections to barometer readings (capillarity) and reduce values to a standard temperature (32°F) before computing monthly means; report corrected means explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report precipitation and monthly totals
rubrics_metrics.description: Rain, in inches. Read off at 9 A.M. ... Sum ... Monthly Mean ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a rain gauge with receiver height reported; read at a standard time (9AM), tabulate daily amounts and compute monthly sums/totals and include these in published tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report qualitative weather remarks alongside numeric entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks column entries: e.g., 'Fine and clear — light brisk wind.' 'A.M. Foggy. P.M. Fine.' 'Overcast and foggy. Light snow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concise qualitative remarks (cloud conditions, precipitation timing, fog, haze, etc.) linked to daily numeric entries to contextualise measurements and note notable weather events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute and present monthly statistical summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean ... Sum ... Monthly Mean of the Barometer ... Monthly Mean (various columns) ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide computed monthly means and sums for recorded variables (barometer, thermometers, rainfall, etc.) and state methods/adjustments used in those computations.
